ArgusML: In-Memory Graph-Powered Observability and Topological Root-Cause Diagnostics for Production Machine Learning Systems

Ghansham Agaldare, Krishna Aher, Akash Kumar, Sanskar Bhargude, Hari Birare
Department of Artificial Intelligence and Data Science
Vishwakarma Institute of Technology (Autonomous Institute Affiliated to Savitribai Phule Pune University), Pune, Maharashtra, India
Project Faculty Guide: Prof. Sheela Chinchmalatpure
Abstract—
Machine learning models in production rarely break with clean stack traces or HTTP error codes. They rot quietly. When incoming feature distributions shift away from baseline training data, model accuracy drops sharply while server CPU, RAM, and response times look completely healthy. Today's monitoring tools make engineers choose between two bad options: standard server tools like Prometheus track hardware health but miss statistical data drift, while dedicated MLOps tools like Evidently AI run slow batch queries over data warehouses hours after bad predictions already reached live users. To solve this, we built ArgusML, an in-process observability watchdog constructed on five classical data structures: a circular FIFO queue for constant-time O(1) ingestion, a double-ended sliding window tracking classification and continuous regression accuracy in O(1) amortized time, an in-memory hash map registry for sub-microsecond baseline lookups, a binary max-heap prioritizing incidents in O(log K) time, and a 4-layer directed acyclic graph (DAG) mapping pipelines, features, models, and microservices. To stop false alarms during continuous hypothesis testing, our drift engine pairs Two-Sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests (D ≥ 0.15, p < 0.05) with Population Stability Index binning (PSI ≥ 0.25), producing zero false alarms across 10,000 nominal test samples. When drift fires, Reverse-BFS traverses upstream along the graph in O(V + E) to pinpoint the broken input feature, while Forward-BFS maps downstream service impact. We retrain candidate models on fused operational data, validate them against a strict 4-step SLA gate, and promote them atomically with zero downtime. On an AMD Ryzen 7 5800H benchmark across 1,000 runs, ArgusML added just 17.0 μs of serving overhead, ran full diagnostic cycles in 0.412 ± 0.034 ms, and recovered churn classification accuracy from 52.4% to 96.1% and housing R2 from 0.41 to 0.94 in under two seconds, within a 14.2 MB memory footprint.
Index Terms—Data Structures & Algorithms, Production Machine Learning, MLOps Observability, Concept Drift, Kolmogorov-Smirnov Test, Population Stability Index, Directed Acyclic Graph, Reverse-BFS, Automated Retraining, Self-Healing Systems.

I. Introduction & Motivation

A. The Silent Failure Problem in Production ML

Traditional software fails loudly. A null pointer crashes a process, a database timeout triggers a 504 gateway error, and an uncaught exception sends an alert straight to an engineer's phone. Machine learning systems fail differently [1], [12]. An inference service predicting telecom churn, fraudulent credit card transactions, or property values can keep returning clean HTTP 200 responses in under 15 ms, perfectly meeting service-level agreements (SLAs), while its actual predictions become completely useless [2].

This silent breakdown occurs because machine learning algorithms rely on static statistical distributions learned during training. Real-world data moves. Macroeconomic changes, shifting user habits, or unnoticed schema bugs in an upstream data pipeline skew feature inputs [2]. Consider what happens when an upstream ETL job shifts incoming transaction amounts by two standard deviations: the fraud model quietly misclassifies high-dollar fraud as harmless purchases, but server monitoring tools like Datadog still display green checkmarks everywhere. The system looks healthy, but the business is hemorrhaging money. Because standard tools only check if a container is alive, corrupted predictions run wild for days or weeks before anyone notices.

B. Why Existing Tools Fall Short

Standard infrastructure monitors like Prometheus and Grafana track server heartbeats, not mathematical probability distributions [3]. They track operating system telemetry: CPU spikes, memory leaks, and network dropouts. If the Python process does not crash, Prometheus thinks everything is fine. It has no way of knowing that an input feature's mean shifted from 50 to 120.

Specialized MLOps tools like Evidently AI, Great Expectations, and Arize tried to tackle this problem [4], [5]. But they share a major architectural bottleneck: they rely on heavy batch database queries against external warehouses like Snowflake or PostgreSQL. Running a Two-Sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test or Population Stability Index binning over SQL tables takes anywhere from 450 to 1,800 ms per query, consumes gigabytes of warehouse memory, and costs real cloud dollars on every scan. Most engineering teams schedule these scans as hourly or nightly cron jobs. That delay is dangerous. In batch setups, poisoned inference outputs hit customers for hours or days before any on-call engineer spots the issue.

C. Research Problem and Design Goals

We asked a direct systems question: Can an observability engine catch statistical drift, walk a dependency graph backward to find the broken feature, and trigger safe model retraining entirely inside system memory—without adding more than a few microseconds of latency to live prediction requests?

We designed ArgusML around four engineering targets:

1) Microsecond Ingestion & Rolling Metrics: Ingest live predictions and update rolling accuracy, F1, R2, and RMSE metrics in O(1) amortized time without blocking client inference threads.
2) In-Memory Statistical Drift Testing: Run Two-Sample KS tests and PSI binning directly over RAM arrays, avoiding slow external database roundtrips.
3) Graph-Based Root Cause Search: When data drifts, walk the pipeline graph backward with Reverse-BFS to isolate the broken upstream feature in under one millisecond.
4) Closed-Loop Model Retraining: Re-fit candidate models on combined baseline and recent window data, enforce a strict 4-step SLA verification gate, and swap the new model version in with zero downtime.

II. Related Work & Literature Review

A. Drift Detection in Streaming Machine Learning

Detecting distribution shift in continuous data streams has followed four main paths: sequential hypothesis testing like Two-Sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) [8], adaptive sliding windows that track error rates [6], quantile divergence binning via Population Stability Index (PSI) [9], and non-parametric distance metrics such as Maximum Mean Discrepancy.

Engineers face two distinct failure modes in production: concept drift, where the underlying target relationship P(y|X) changes, versus covariate shift, where input feature distributions P(X) move while label mappings stay intact [2], [6]. Catching concept drift in real time is rarely feasible in live production because true labels y arrive with long delays—credit card chargebacks take weeks to clear, and churn confirmations only appear after subscription cycles end. Live monitors must rely primarily on unsupervised covariate shift detection across incoming feature vectors X. Rabanser et al. [10] showed that univariate two-sample tests uncover feature corruption reliably with much lower compute overhead than multivariate kernel embeddings. ArgusML pairs Two-Sample KS testing with PSI quantile binning: KS provides sensitive detection of local cumulative probability gaps in O(W log W), while PSI tracks macro quantile redistribution across bins in O(W + B).

B. Data Quality, Lineage, and Root-Cause Diagnostics

Data validation tools have emerged across industry. Google's TensorFlow Data Validation (TFDV) [13] checks pipeline schemas on Apache Beam, while Amazon Deequ [14] runs unit tests on Apache Spark clusters. Alibi-Detect [15] provides standalone inference filters, and MLflow [16] logs experiment parameters and model artifacts.

In diagnostic literature, contrastive explanations [19] analyze which feature subspaces explain distribution divergence, while microservice tracing tools [18] isolate RPC latency anomalies along call trees. But these platforms operate as detached offline jobs: TFDV and Deequ require heavy cluster processing, Alibi-Detect inspects models without tracking upstream data lineage, and MLflow stores static metadata without watching live streaming distributions. Past tools treated drift checking, causal graph tracing, and model retraining as separate, unconnected projects.

C. Incident Prioritization & Alert Fatigue

Cascading alert storms make things worse in production [7]. When an upstream ETL job breaks, it rarely affects just one feature. The bad data ripples across multiple features, models, and downstream APIs. When teams store incident tickets in basic FIFO lists, cascade noise swamps engineers while the real upstream root cause stays hidden.

Prioritizing alerts by a composite severity score surfaces the most critical failure immediately. ArgusML implements this via an array-backed binary max-heap [11], keeping the highest-priority incident at the heap root with logarithmic O(log K) insertions and extractions, completely eliminating external message broker dependencies for local alert ordering.

The Missing Link: Existing research treats drift detection, graph lineage, and model retraining as separate tools. Drift checkers spot data changes without knowing which pipeline broke; distributed tracing tools map microservices without checking probability distributions; and alerting tools rarely fix models safely. ArgusML brings all three together inside a single, fast, in-process runtime built on classic computer science data structures.

III. System Architecture & 5-Plane Topology

A. Overview of System Planes

Fig. 1 shows the overall system design. We structured ArgusML into five functional planes, each backed by a specific data structure:

1) Ingestion Plane: Asynchronous REST endpoints accept incoming prediction requests and push them into an in-memory circular FIFO buffer.
2) Fast Telemetry Kernel: The queue feeds a double-ended sliding window that maintains running confusion matrix accumulators (classification) or residual error sums (regression) in O(1) amortized time.
3) Statistical Drift Engine: A background worker processes windowed data every 25 predictions, computing Two-Sample KS and PSI statistics against baseline distributions retrieved from a fast hash map.
4) Graph Diagnostics & Triage: Upon confirming drift, a 4-layer DAG launches Reverse-BFS to isolate the damaged feature and pipeline, and Forward-BFS to measure downstream blast radius. A binary max-heap orders incident tickets by composite severity.
5) Self-Healing & Audit Trail: Confirmed drift alerts trigger model retraining on fused data, validate candidate models against SLA gates, promote versions atomically, and persist post-mortem logs.

B. Decoupling Serving Latency from Analytical Processing

To protect client inference latencies, execution is split into two asynchronous paths. The fast serving path (circular queue ingestion and sliding window accumulator updates) runs inline on the prediction request thread, adding only 17.0 μs of overhead. The slow analytical path (array sorting for KS tests, quantile binning for PSI, DAG traversals, and heap operations) executes on a background thread every 25 incoming samples. This separation ensures that deep diagnostic checks never degrade active inference throughput.

IV. Foundational DSA Telemetry Kernel & Mathematical Formulation

A. Circular FIFO Event Queue

We build the circular ingestion buffer around a fixed-capacity array, advancing two integer pointers (head and tail) with modular arithmetic (backend/app/core/dsa/queue.py):

head ← (head + 1) mod C,   tail ← (tail + 1) mod C

We pre-allocated an array of capacity C = 5,000 so incoming prediction bursts are absorbed without repeatedly creating new heap objects. This avoids Python garbage collection pauses during heavy traffic surges. Both enqueue and dequeue execute in guaranteed O(1) time.

B. Metric Sliding Window (Deque)

Rescanning historical predictions on every calculation wastes compute. Instead, ArgusML keeps running confusion matrices and error sums in an in-memory double-ended queue (backend/app/core/dsa/deque.py). For classification models, the deque tracks true positives (TP), false positives (FP), true negatives (TN), and false negatives (FN):

Accuracy = (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN)
Precision = TP / (TP + FP),   Recall = TP / (TP + FN)

When a new prediction arrives, its classification outcome increments the matching counter. When the window reaches capacity (default W = 400), the deque drops the oldest sample from its head and subtracts its values from running tallies in O(1) amortized time. For continuous regression models, running accumulators track the sum of actual values ∑yi, sum of squared actual values ∑yi2, and sum of squared residuals SSR = ∑(yi − ŷi)2:

R2 = 1 − (SSR / SST),   RMSE = √(SSR / W)

where total sum of squares SST = ∑yi2 − (∑yi)2 / W. These updates take O(1) amortized time without re-evaluating past observations.

C. Hash Map Model Registry

We index model metadata, operational SLA thresholds, and empirical baseline distributions in an in-memory hash map keyed by model identifier (backend/app/core/dsa/registry.py). Lookups execute in average-case O(1) time (measured at 0.8 μs in empirical profiling), enabling instant reference baseline lookups during drift evaluations.

D. Statistical Drift Detection Kernel

ArgusML combines two complementary non-parametric statistical metrics to evaluate distribution stability over sliding window observations:

1) Two-Sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov Test: Measures the maximum divergence between the baseline empirical cumulative distribution function Fbase(x) and the streaming live distribution Flive(x) (Fig. 2(a)):

Dn,m = supx |Fbase(x) − Flive(x)|

2) Population Stability Index (PSI): Bins baseline distributions into B = 10 quantiles and measures distribution divergence against live frequencies (Fig. 2(b)):

PSI = ∑b=1B (Ab − Eb) × ln((Ab + ε) / (Eb + ε))

Window Size Selection and Benjamini-Hochberg (FDR) Multi-Testing Control: Choosing the sliding window capacity W = 400 balances sample stability against reaction speed. Across experimental trials evaluating window sizes from W = 50 to W = 2,000, smaller windows (W < 150) reacted quickly to sharp step shifts but exhibited high sampling variance, causing occasional false alerts under normal streaming noise. Larger windows (W > 1,000) smoothed out sample noise but introduced physical detection lag and raised array sorting time from 0.21 ms to 1.84 ms. We chose W = 400 as the practical operating point: it provides at least 40 samples per decile bin for stable PSI calculations while keeping evaluation times well under one millisecond. In streaming environments, continuous hypothesis testing across high-dimensional feature spaces (M ≥ 30) risks family-wise alpha inflation (Pfamily = 1 − (1 − α)M). To stamp out false positive spikes across wide schemas, ArgusML applies the algorithmic Benjamini-Hochberg False Discovery Rate (FDR) procedure: we rank feature p-values ascending P(1) ≤ &dots; ≤ P(M) and thresholded against adaptive critical boundaries P(k) ≤ (k / M) Q (with Q = 0.05). We enforce a conjunctive dual-gate filter requiring both an FDR-confirmed KS statistic (D ≥ 0.15, padj < 0.05) and binned PSI quantile divergence (PSI ≥ 0.10 for warning, ≥ 0.25 for critical). In our baseline test runs, this dual-gate setup yielded zero false alerts across 10,000 consecutive nominal predictions.

Fig. 2. Statistical feature drift characterization: (a) Empirical Cumulative Distribution Functions (ECDF) exhibiting significant divergence (KS statistic D = 0.482, p < 0.001); (b) Population Stability Index (PSI = 0.341) exceeding critical operational threshold.

E. Alert Max-Heap Priority Queue

Alert floods overwhelm on-call engineers. To prevent this, active alerts sit in an array-backed binary max-heap (backend/app/core/dsa/heap.py) using pure _sift_up and _sift_down logic. Each incident receives a composite severity score σ:

σ = 0.40 × (1 − Acc) + 0.35 × (PSI / 0.50) + 0.25 × (LatP99 / SLAlat)

The binary max-heap property ensures that the root element always stores the most severe incident:

Heap[parent(i)].σ ≥ Heap[i].σ,   ∀ i > 0

Insertions and extractions run in guaranteed O(log K) time, providing steady performance even when multiple components experience issues simultaneously.

V. In-Memory Dependency Graph & Topological Root-Cause Diagnostics

A. Building the 4-Layer Dependency DAG

We structure the runtime architecture as a Directed Acyclic Graph G = (V, E) across four distinct functional tiers (backend/app/core/dsa/graph.py):

• Layer 1 – Pipelines: Ingestion sources (e.g., telecom_billing_pipeline, crm_export_pipeline).
• Layer 2 – Features: Individual model input columns (e.g., total_day_minutes, customer_service_calls). Edges link each feature to its upstream ingestion pipeline.
• Layer 3 – Model: The deployed inference model artifact (customer_churn_v1).
• Layer 4 – Services: Downstream consumer microservices that consume predictions (retention_campaign_service, billing_api).

Fig. 3. Topological Reverse-BFS root-cause attribution and Forward-BFS blast radius traversal over the 4-layer dependency graph, isolating the corrupted upstream pipeline.

B. Reverse-BFS Upstream Candidate Attribution

When a model degrades, Reverse-BFS climbs backward along incoming graph edges from Layer 3 into Layer 2. It tests each feeding feature against baseline distributions. ArgusML isolates whichever feature displays the steepest statistical divergence as the prime culprit.

Algorithm 1: Reverse-BFS Upstream Candidate Attribution Input: DependencyGraph G=(V,E), ModelNode m Output: CulpritFeature c*, UpstreamPipeline p* 1: Queue Q ← empty, Visited ← empty, Candidates ← empty 2: Q.enqueue(m), Visited.add(m) 3: while Q is not empty do 4: curr ← Q.dequeue() 5: for each u ∈ G.in_edges(curr) do 6: if u ∉ Visited then 7: Visited.add(u) 8: if u.type == FEATURE and u.drift_score > θ then 9: Candidates.append((u, u.drift_score)) 10: Q.enqueue(u) 11: c* ← argmax(Candidates, key=λx: x.drift_score) 12: p* ← G.in_edges(c*) 13: return c*, p*

Handling Multi-Feature Pipeline Failures: In production systems, an upstream schema error or broken ETL task often corrupts multiple features at the same time. In these scenarios, Reverse-BFS travels backward from the model node, evaluates all feeding features, and identifies each drifted input. Because the DAG maps features to their originating ingestion pipelines (Layer 2 ← Layer 1), multiple concurrently drifting features naturally point to their common parent pipeline in Layer 1. This lets ArgusML consolidate what would otherwise be a flood of separate feature warnings into a single, actionable pipeline incident.

Statistical Attribution vs. Causal Inference: We note that this topological walk follows operational telemetry links rather than formal causal discovery like Pearl's do-calculus [17]. Reverse-BFS follows physical data pipeline lineage edges (Model ← Features ← Pipelines) to pinpoint which ingestion pathway supplied the drifted inputs. ArgusML crowns whichever feature exhibits the sharpest statistical deviation as prime culprit. While this isolated the true corrupted pipeline with 100% precision in our benchmark experiments, it represents distributional attribution across known data paths rather than counterfactual proof.

C. Forward-BFS Blast Radius Quantification

On-call engineers troubleshooting an outage need to know which customer services suffer degradation. Forward-BFS follows outgoing edges from Layer 3 into Layer 4 to identify all dependent microservices. We measure blast radius as the exact fraction of downstream consumers impacted across total registered services. In our telecom benchmark, a fault in total_day_minutes traversed forward to flag both retention_campaign_service and billing_api within 32 μs.

VI. Closed-Loop Self-Healing & Automated Model Retraining

A. Dual-Dataset Fusion & Data Leakage Prevention

Waiting for manual retraining leaves broken models serving live traffic for days. ArgusML automates closed-loop retraining by combining historical training baselines with recent sliding-window records:

Dretrain = Dbase ∪ Dlive

Separating Unsupervised Telemetry from Supervised Retraining: In live environments, true labels often take significant time to arrive (such as 30 to 90 days for customer churn confirmations or resolved chargebacks). ArgusML purposefully isolates statistical drift detection from the retraining pipeline. Drift monitoring, Reverse-BFS root-cause tracing, and blast radius analysis run completely unsupervised over incoming feature vectors in real time without needing labels. The system triggers retraining only after verified ground-truth labels arrive in operational batch stores or an engineer confirms the incident ticket.

Dataset Splitting and Preventing Data Leakage: In live environments, Dlive captures recent streaming telemetry whose ground-truth labels have cleared verification. To avoid optimistic bias and guarantee honest evaluation, the retrainer validates candidate models against an independent held-out split Dtest (20% of baseline records) held completely separate from both Dbase and Dlive. This ensures that reported accuracy and R2 recovery numbers reflect true generalization to unseen samples rather than memorization of the retraining set.

Auditable Provenance & Exportable Retraining Artifacts: Upon fusing Dbase and Dlive, the engine tags every row with an immutable _provenance attribute (distinguishing baseline historical data from live streaming telemetry). To support regulatory compliance (e.g. EU AI Act auditability) and reproducible offline verification, ArgusML exposes an automated dataset export endpoint (GET /api/models/{model_id}/export-dataset), serializing the versioned CSV artifact alongside incident post-mortems.

B. 4-Step Validation Gate & Semantic Version Promotion

Candidate models are refit (using algorithms such as Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, or Ridge Regression) and evaluated against four sequential gates: (i) SLA Threshold: candidate accuracy ≥ 85% or R2 ≥ 0.80; (ii) Drift Improvement: candidate metric ≥ active model score − 0.02; (iii) Latency SLA: P99 inference latency ≤ 200 ms; and (iv) Numerical Validity: all evaluation metrics finite and non-NaN. If all four gates pass, the registry promotes the candidate atomically and increments the semantic version number (v1.0.0 → v1.1.0).

C. Baseline Recalibration & Alert Resolution

Following atomic promotion of the candidate model, ArgusML updates reference baseline distributions directly from Dretrain, pops the resolved alert from the max-heap, and resets affected DAG nodes back to HEALTHY.

D. Post-Mortem Generation & Audit Trail

Each resolved incident generates an exportable Markdown post-mortem detailing the root cause attribution, statistical indicators (KS statistic D, PSI), affected downstream services, and before/after performance numbers. An append-only session drawer records all model registrations, alerts, and retraining events alongside reproducible DAG topology snapshots.

VII. Empirical Evaluation & Benchmarking

A. Experimental Setup and Hardware Details

We executed all benchmarks on a physical AMD Ryzen 7 5800H CPU @ 3.20 GHz (8 cores, 16 threads) with 16 GB DDR4 RAM running 64-bit Windows 11 Pro and Python 3.13.2 with NumPy 1.26.4 and SciPy 1.13.1. Testing covered three domain datasets: Telecom Churn (N = 7,043, d = 20), Credit Card Fraud (N = 10,000, d = 14), and Real Estate Valuation (N = 500, d = 4). We clocked all execution stages using high-resolution monotonic hardware timers (time.perf_counter_ns()) across 1,000 consecutive runs, discarding the initial 50 warm-up runs to remove JIT and cache priming noise. We express all measurements as Mean ± Standard Deviation.

Architectural Context of Comparisons: To ensure a fair comparison, we note the architectural context of the evaluated baselines. We profiled Evidently AI via batch Python DataFrame sweeps, and Prometheus across network HTTP pull scrapes. ArgusML runs entirely in memory without inter-process communication (IPC) or socket serialization. The comparison highlights the efficiency gains of keeping the telemetry kernel in-process compared to external database- and network-bound tools.

B. Ingestion Throughput Scalability

Fig. 4 plots end-to-end ingestion latency as throughput scaled from 100 to 10,000 predictions/sec. Mean processing time remained stable at 0.412 ± 0.034 ms. The circular FIFO buffer absorbs spikes without thread contention, maintaining sub-millisecond latencies across streaming loads.

C. Component-Level Ablation Study

To evaluate the practical benefit of each algorithmic design choice, we performed an ablation study across three dimensions: drift detection method, culprit search strategy, and retraining dataset composition (Table III).

TABLE III: Component-Level Ablation Study (10,000 Streaming Events)
Ablation Dimension Evaluated Configuration Attribution Precision False Alert Rate
Drift Detection Strategy Two-Sample KS Only 94.2% 6.8% (Sample Noise)
PSI Quantile Binning Only 88.6% 4.1%
Dual Gate: KS + PSI (Ours) 100.0% 0.0% (Zero False Alarms)
Culprit Search Strategy Linear Scan (All Features) 100.0% (0.84 ms) N/A (No Lineage)
Reverse-BFS DAG (Ours) 100.0% (0.18 ms) Traces Pipeline Origin
Retraining Dataset Live Window Only (Dlive) 81.4% (Catastrophic Forget) N/A
Dual Fusion (Dbase ∪ Dlive) 96.1% (Generalizing) Robust to Prior Baseline

As Table III shows, combining the KS test with PSI quantile binning eliminated the 6.8% false positive rate observed when running KS tests alone, while fusing baseline and live data prevented the model from forgetting older historical patterns. ArgusML achieved 100% culprit-attribution precision across our controlled covariate shift injection scenarios.

Fig. 5 illustrates the recovery behavior following drift detection. In the churn benchmark, injecting a 2.5× covariate shift into total_day_minutes reduced model accuracy from 95.8% to 52.4%. The max-heap registered a critical alert, and automated retraining on the fused dataset fit a recovered model in 420 ms. Evaluated on the held-out test split, classification accuracy returned to 96.1% (Table IV).

VIII. Controlled Multi-Domain Evaluation Across Benchmark Case Studies

A. Telecom Churn (Classification)

The primary classification benchmark used the IBM Telecom Churn dataset (7,043 samples, 20 features). After 200 normal prediction calls, we injected a synthetic covariate shift by multiplying total_day_minutes by 2.5×. The KS statistic jumped immediately to D = 0.482 (p < 0.001) with a PSI of 0.341. Reverse-BFS tracked the root fault back to telecom_billing_pipeline, Forward-BFS alerted retention_campaign_service, and automated retraining brought model accuracy from 52.4% back up to 96.1%.

B. Credit Card Fraud (Imbalanced Stream)

We evaluated an imbalanced fraud stream (99.8% legitimate, 0.2% fraud). Artificially inflating transaction amounts by 3.0× shifted the feature distribution, triggering an alert with priority score σ = 94.2. Reverse-BFS isolated transaction_amount in 0.17 ms, identifying the problem before silent fraud leakage could continue unnoticed.

C. Real Estate Valuation (Continuous Regression)

We tested continuous real estate pricing using 4 features and 500 records. Shifting square_footage dropped the model's R2 from 0.94 to 0.41 and increased RMSE to $58,000. Closed-loop retraining refit Ridge Regression and brought R2 back to 0.94 ($22,000 RMSE), proving that sliding-window residual tracking supports continuous regression models with equal precision.

Controlled Testing Limitations: While ArgusML achieved 100% culprit-attribution precision across these controlled tests, real-world systems may face unmeasured confounding variables, third-party network dependencies, or simultaneous multi-source failures that need broader graph modeling.

IX. Architectural Discussion & Future Work

A. Engineering Trade-offs

Our architecture intentionally trades bounded memory capacity for instantaneous sub-millisecond diagnosis. Setting the sliding window capacity to W = 400 limits memory consumption to a compact 14.2 MB. When compliance policies demand multi-month archival logs, workers stream window snapshots asynchronously to cold cloud storage without slowing the in-memory telemetry kernel.

B. Limitations and Next Steps

Future work will explore three directions: (i) multi-node Raft consensus to synchronize monitoring state across Kubernetes clusters; (ii) webhook integrations for Slack and PagerDuty notifications; and (iii) scaling the Reverse-BFS engine for high-dimensional feature spaces (such as recommendation systems with thousands of sparse embeddings). In those larger models, a fast initial filter based on feature variance or mean shift can quickly prune dormant features before running full distribution comparisons.

X. Conclusion

Machine learning observability should not require gigabytes of database bloat or hours of batch delay. In this paper, we built ArgusML around five foundational computer science data structures: circular FIFO queues, double-ended sliding windows, hash maps, binary max-heaps, and directed acyclic graphs. By pairing dual-gate KS and PSI drift testing with Reverse-BFS dependency tracing and a 4-step retraining gate, ArgusML achieves 0.412 ms end-to-end ingestion, 0.184 ms culprit feature isolation, and automated self-healing recovery—all within a compact 14.2 MB RAM footprint. These empirical benchmarks prove that deterministic, in-memory algorithmic engineering delivers rock-solid AI observability without the bloat of distributed clusters.
